The discovery of Sagittarius A*, also known as Sgr A* (SAG-tar-ri-si-us AH-star), began in 1974 with Bruce Balick and Robert L. Brown. The black hole was discovered using the Very Large Array, a network of radio telescopes located across North America. It is located near the border of the constellations Sagittarius and Scorpius, about 5.6° south of the ecliptic, visually close to the Butterfly Cluster (M6) and Lambda Scorpii.

In May 2022, astronomers released a first image of the accretion disk around the event horizon of Sagittarius A* using the Event Horizon Telescope, a world-wide network of radio observatories. This is the second confirmed image of a black hole after Messier 87's supermassive black hole in 2019. The black hole itself is not seen; only objects influenced by its gravity are visible.

Sgr A* was discovered and named by Bruce Balick, who understood that strong radio emission emanates from gas and dust heated to millions of degrees while falling into the black hole. The discovery has been a significant breakthrough in astrophysics, as it provides an opportunity to study one of the most extreme environments in the universe.
